title: Berkshire 1999 letter: a "D" year, float economics, and why buybacks only work below intrinsic value
summary: Buffett owns a poor 1999 as the worst year of his tenure, then teaches how to value insurance float, why managers run Berkshire companies like family assets, how to think about goodwill and acquisitions, circle of competence on tech, and strict rules for share repurchases.

principles.text: Judge an insurer by float volume, its cost, and above all the long-term outlook for both.
principles.quote: The key determinants are: (1) the amount of float that the business generates; (2) its cost; and (3) most critical of all, the long-term outlook for both of these factors.

principles.text: Float is worth having only if its cost is below what you would pay for money elsewhere.
principles.quote: An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds. But the business is a lemon if its cost of float is higher than market rates for money.

principles.text: Stay inside your circle of competence; don't pretend to predict fast-changing industries.
principles.quote: If we have a strength, it is in recognizing when we are operating well within our circle of competence and when we are approaching the perimeter.

principles.text: Repurchase shares only with spare funds and when the stock trades below conservatively calculated intrinsic value.
principles.quote: There is only one combination of facts that makes it advisable for a company to repurchase its shares: First, the company has available funds — cash plus sensible borrowing capacity — beyond the near-term needs of the business and, second, finds its stock selling in the market below its intrinsic value, conservatively-calculated.

principles.text: Overpaying to buy back stock hurts the shareholders who stay.
principles.quote: But the continuing shareholder is penalized by repurchases above intrinsic value. Buying dollar bills for $1.10 is not good business for those who stick around.

principles.text: Give managers autonomy and ask them to run the business as their family's only asset for a century.
principles.quote: We simply ask our managers to run their companies as if these are the sole asset of their families and will remain so for the next century.
